transcript.text: Sometimes when I open the dishwasher there's grey smelly water in the bottom even though it finished draining fine. Not every day though. Kitchen sink was replaced last month if that matters.

That grey, smelly water left in the bottom after a cycle usually means the dishwasher didn't fully clear its own drainage path, allowing dirty water to sit and stagnate until you open the door. Given your kitchen sink was replaced recently, there are two common culprits: either the filter inside the machine is blocked with debris, or the connection at the new sink waste has a small blanking plug left in place (which blocks the drain hose). Let's start with the most likely and easiest fix. 1. Turn off the dishwasher and unplug it for safety.
2. Remove the lower rack to access the filter assembly at the bottom of the tub.
3. Twist and lift out the main filter (and any coarse mesh filter if present).
4. Rinse the filter under the tap and clear away any food or grease.
5. Look into the sump (the hole underneath where the filter was) with a torch. Check for any foreign objects like glass, stones, or bone fragments that might be blocking the drain pump impeller.
[Helpful to see: image "Where the filter is" — The filter sits in the base of the dishwasher, usually under the bottom spray arm. Twist it out anticlockwise and rinse it under a tap. Typical layout — your dishwasher may differ.]
Ok, I've taken the filter out and it's clean, nothing in the sump that I can see. It tends to happen after I drain the sink full of washing-up water, if that helps. The sink drains a little slow too.

That pattern—water appearing specifically after you drain a full sink of soapy water, combined with the slow-draining sink—is a classic sign that the dishwasher is drawing dirty water back up its drain hose because the sink waste isn't clearing fast enough. Since your filter and sump are clean, the blockage or restriction is likely at the connection point under the sink. Please check two things:
1. Under the sink, locate where the dishwasher's grey drain hose connects to the new sink waste unit. If it connects into a spigot (a small outlet on the side of the waste), ensure that any plastic blanking plug inside that spigot has been removed or cut out. If it is still in place, water cannot flow freely and will back up.
2. Run the kitchen tap at full speed. Does the sink drain quickly, or does it pool? A slow-draining sink trap can cause exactly this issue. If you find a blanking plug was left in, remove it (you may need pliers) and ensure the hose is pushed firmly onto the spigot. If the sink itself drains slowly, you may need to clean the sink's P-trap or call a plumber if the new installation has an issue. Let me know what you find with the blanking plug and the sink drainage speed.

I had a look under the sink. The hose just lies on the cupboard floor and goes straight into the waste spigot, no high loop at all (the fitter did that when the new sink went in). I didn't see a blanking plug mentioned anywhere, not sure how to tell if there's one inside. The sink does drain a little slow, yes.

The evidence points to the dishwasher drawing dirty water back in from the sink because there is no 'high loop' on the drain hose. When you drain a full sink of soapy water, the pressure pushes that dirty water up the dishwasher's drain hose and into the machine, where it sits until the next cycle starts (or leaks out when you open the door). The slow-draining sink makes this worse. This is a plumbing installation issue, not a fault with the dishwasher itself. To fix it: 1. Pull the dishwasher out carefully (turn off and unplug first).
2. Lift the drain hose so it arches up to at least 60cm above the floor level before going down into the sink waste spigot.
3. Secure this high point with a clip or tie it to the underside of the worktop or the top of the cabinet frame. Do not let it rest on the cupboard floor. If you cannot create this height, the water will continue to siphon back in every time you drain soapy water. If you do create the loop and the problem stops, that suggests the cause. If the sink itself remains very slow to drain even after clearing any debris from the trap, you may also need a plumber to check the new waste installation for a partial blockage.
I've looped the hose up high and clipped it under the worktop, and the dirty water hasn't come back since. The sink still drains a little slow though, is that something I should get looked at?

The dirty water was siphoning back in because of that low loop, so keeping it elevated stops the problem from happening again. Regarding the slow-draining sink: yes, you should get that looked at. Even with the dishwasher fixed, a slow drain means waste is sitting in your pipes longer than it should, which can lead to blockages or bad smells later on. It sounds like the new installation might have a slight restriction (perhaps a partially blocked trap or an issue with the waste unit itself), so calling the fitter back to check it is the right move.
